title: Can you structure these 13 cost reduction case questions in two minutes each?
description: 13 cost reduction case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes, if you bring discipline to every prompt: break the cost into its drivers, go to the biggest pool first, and never cut what brings in revenue. Cost cases punish long lists of savings ideas and reward candidates who size the cost base before suggesting anything. Here are 13 prompts: two minutes each, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
How to use this set

Give yourself two minutes per prompt. A good cost structure usually does one of two things: splits the cost into a formula (number of returns × cost per return) or splits the cost base into its biggest pools (staff, property, technology, suppliers). Then say which branch you would size first. The model shows the buckets, the starting point and the trap. For the method, read how to structure a cost-cutting case and where to look for cost savings.

1. A fashion retailer's online returns now cost $40M a year, double three years ago.

Show a model structure
  • Number of returns: online orders (did sales grow?); return rate by category, size and brand; serial returners.
  • Cost per return: shipping, handling and refurbishing; items that can no longer be sold.
  • Why customers return: fit and sizing, photos and descriptions; ordering several sizes on purpose.
  • Policy: free returns and the return window; charging, store returns, offering exchanges first.

Where to start: orders × return rate × cost per return. Find which of the three grew, then which categories drive it.

The trap: listing policies to change before splitting the number of returns from the cost per return.

2. A retail bank wants to cut operating costs by 15% in two years.

Show a model structure
  • Branches: number, size and use; staffing against footfall.
  • Operations: payments, lending and account opening; automation and outsourcing.
  • Technology: old systems, licences and data centres; duplicate apps and vendors.
  • Support functions: HR, finance and procurement; management layers.

Where to start: the biggest cost pool first, usually staff in branches and operations.

The trap: listing ideas without sizing the cost base, so you cannot say which matter.

3. A food-delivery start-up is burning $5M a month. Where would you cut?

Show a model structure
  • Unit economics per order: commission, delivery fee and courier cost; discounts and refunds.
  • Marketing: cost to acquire a customer against their value; promotions with no repeat orders.
  • Cities: profit by city; pausing or exiting the weakest.
  • Fixed costs: head office, technology and offices; hiring plans.

Where to start: profit per order by city. If every order loses money, more volume makes it worse.

The trap: cutting head office first when the loss is built into every order.

4. A bakery chain throws away 15% of what it bakes.

Show a model structure
  • What is wasted: by product, store and day; fresh versus packaged.
  • Forecasting: how stores decide quantities; weather, events and promotions.
  • Production: batch sizes and minimum orders; baking once versus through the day.
  • Selling it off: end-of-day discounts and donations; surplus-food apps.

Where to start: forecasting. Waste often comes from baking for the best day, every day.

The trap: cutting the range before fixing how much is baked.

5. An energy supplier's unpaid bills have doubled.

Show a model structure
  • Who is not paying: segment and payment method; new versus long-standing customers.
  • Why: higher bills and cost of living; billing errors and estimated readings.
  • Collections: how quickly we chase; payment plans offered.
  • Prevention: prepayment and smart meters; checks when customers join.

Where to start: who is not paying. Hardship and billing errors need different responses.

The trap: chasing harder without separating customers who cannot pay from those who will not.

6. An online furniture retailer's delivery cost per order rose 40%.

Show a model structure
  • Orders: size and weight; share needing two-person delivery.
  • Routes: drops per van per day; distance between drops and rural share.
  • Failures: failed deliveries and returns; damage in transit.
  • Rates: carrier prices and fuel; own fleet versus third party.

Where to start: drops per van. Route density usually explains most of the cost per order.

The trap: renegotiating carrier rates while failed deliveries keep rising.

7. Should a bank close a third of its branches?

Show a model structure
  • Usage: visits and transactions per branch; who still uses branches.
  • Savings: rent, staff and maintenance per branch; one-off closure costs.
  • Customer impact: customers who might leave; vulnerable customers and rural areas.
  • Alternatives: shared branches and post offices; mobile and video banking.

Where to start: usage. Which branches have few visits and another branch nearby?

The trap: closing on cost alone without checking which customers, and how much revenue, would leave.

8. How can a hospital cut costs by 5% without harming patient care?

Show a model structure
  • Staff: agency versus permanent staff; rostering to demand.
  • Supplies and drugs: joint buying and cheaper equivalents; waste and stock.
  • Patient flow: length of stay and cancelled operations; theatre utilisation.
  • Estate and back office: energy and buildings; admin and IT.

Where to start: agency staff, usually the most expensive way to fill a shift.

The trap: cutting front-line staff numbers instead of changing how staff are used.

9. How could a supermarket chain cut its energy use by 20%?

Show a model structure
  • Refrigeration: doors on fridges and efficient units; maintenance and leaks.
  • Lighting and heating: LEDs and controls; heat recovered from fridges.
  • Buildings: insulation and solar panels; store design.
  • Behaviour and data: meters per store; targets and training.

Where to start: refrigeration, usually the biggest energy user in a supermarket.

The trap: starting with lighting because it is easy.

10. How can a retailer cut theft and stock losses by half?

Show a model structure
  • Where losses happen: stores, products and times; theft versus errors versus damage.
  • External theft: security, tags and layout; self-checkout controls.
  • Internal: staff theft and processes; audits.
  • Errors and damage: deliveries, pricing and waste; stock counting.

Where to start: where losses happen. A few stores and products usually account for most of it.

The trap: adding guards everywhere.

11. A haulier's trucks run empty 30% of the time. How can it reduce that?

Show a model structure
  • Where empty miles happen: return legs, regions and days; customers with one-way flows.
  • Find loads: freight exchanges and partners; selling to fill return legs.
  • Plan better: route planning and combining loads; depot locations.
  • Price: discounts for return loads; contracts that pay for empty legs.

Where to start: where empty miles happen, often return legs on a few routes.

The trap: buying planning software when the real gap is customers to fill the trucks.

12. How can a hotel group cut costs by 10% without guests noticing?

Show a model structure
  • Staff: rostering to occupancy; shared roles across hotels.
  • Rooms: laundry, amenities and energy; linen changes on longer stays.
  • Food and drink: menus, waste and suppliers; breakfast set-up.
  • Central costs: joint buying; technology and marketing.

Where to start: staff rostered to occupancy, the biggest cost that can move with demand.

The trap: cutting things guests do notice, such as room quality.

13. How can a fashion retailer cut the stock it sells at discount from 40% to 25%?

Show a model structure
  • Buying: fewer lines and smaller first orders; better forecasts.
  • Speed: faster suppliers and repeat orders; testing before buying big.
  • Allocation: the right sizes to the right stores; moving stock between stores.
  • Pricing: smaller discounts given earlier; outlets and resale.

Where to start: buying. Most markdowns are decided when the stock is ordered.

The trap: focusing on clearance tactics instead of buying less.

How to score your answer: gross versus real savings

Take the returns prompt. Suppose you propose better size guides and expect 10% fewer returns. It is tempting to claim 10% of $40M, or $4M. But some return costs are fixed in the short term, such as the warehouse space and the team that runs it. If 70% of the cost is variable, the immediate saving is 10% × 70% × $40M = $2.8M, before the cost of building the size guides.

Check two more things. First, revenue: a harsh returns policy can cut return costs while losing more in sales. Second, double counting: better size guides and better product photos both reduce returns, so you cannot claim the same saved returns for each.

When you compare with the model, mark whether you sized the cost before suggesting cuts, whether you protected revenue, and whether your first step was the biggest pool.
